Orioles bring back center fielder Robert on one-year deal
The deal: One year, $12 million Grade: C

It's been three seasons of injuries and subpar results since Luis Robert Jr. had his big year in 2023 for the Chicago White Sox, when he hit .264 with 38 home runs, 75 extra-base hits and plus defense in center field. Yet we still dream the magic will somehow return, even as he now enters his age-29 season. The Baltimore Orioles are certainly dreaming big, believing Robert can be their full-time center fielder in 2027.

The best guess here: It's unlikely to happen. There's nothing from the past three seasons that suggests Robert can stay healthy and also hit the way he did in 2023. Over the past three seasons, averaging 90 games per season, he has hit .223/.290/.379 for a subpar OPS+ of 88. That includes three games in 2026 with the Orioles, who claimed him off waivers from the Mets in August -- only to see Robert immediately go down with a hamstring injury.

That didn't scare them off. Look, Robert is enticing. He still has power and is still capable of playing at least a decent center field -- two attributes the Orioles didn't get from their center fielders in 2026. The Orioles ranked tied for 23rd in the majors with 12 home runs (and ranked 22nd with a .663 OPS). They ranked 24th in Statcast's fielding runs. But is Robert much of an upgrade? He has a .669 OPS over the past three seasons, and his defensive metrics peaked in 2023.

The $12 million is a bet that he'll play better. Look, it's probably a better roll of the dice than, say, giving Leody Taveras 482 plate appearances, which is what the Orioles did this past season. At least there's a chance Robert might explode with a 30-homer season. His poor approach at the plate is going to limit his offensive output, though; even when he has been more selective, it hasn't translated to better results, leading to low batting averages and low on-base percentages.

We'll give this one a C grade, acknowledging that if Robert can somehow stay healthy, he's still capable of -- if not matching what he did in 2023 -- at least producing a 2.0-WAR season, which would make him an average regular. For $12 million, that would make for a reasonable investment. But it's a big "if" on whether he can stay on the field. -- Schoenfield

Guardians bring back starter Griffin on three-year deal
The deal: Three years, $48 million

Grade: C

Foster Griffin re-signing with the Cleveland Guardians is one of the more surprising transactions during this rush of starting pitchers locking up deals in the final week before the expected lockout freezes all signings. First off, Cleveland just signed Kris Bubic the other day for a one-year, $17.5 million deal -- and he was the sixth starter with last year's group all returning. Griffin now makes it seven potential starters.

Griffin's deal is also tied for the third-biggest free agent signing in franchise history, behind Edwin Encarnacion's $60 million deal and Nick Swisher's $56 million deal (Griffin is tied with Michael Bourn!). That makes Griffin the most expensive free agent pitcher signing for Cleveland -- remarkably, the previous record was Chuck Finley, who signed for $27 million way back in 2000.

So, this is an unusual move for the Guardians. That doesn't make it a bad one. Indeed, Griffin returned from three years in Japan on a one-year deal with the Nationals and made the All-Star team (technically he was still an MLB rookie at 30 years old since he had pitched only briefly in the majors before heading overseas). The Nationals flipped Griffin at the deadline, and even though the results weren't great with Cleveland -- 3-3, 5.19 ERA, 55 hits in 43 innings -- management obviously saw enough to bring him back.

Griffin certainly isn't overpowering, with a 91-92 mph fastball, and actually throws his cutter the most of his seven pitches. Indeed, he's an old-school crafty left-hander who pounds the zone and mixes it up. He uses his four-seamer and sinker more as secondary weapons and both were effective, batters hitting .211 against the four-seamer and .192 against the sinker. It's an unusual profile in today's game, but there's no reason he can't be successful the next three years.

While there's nothing wrong with having seven starters on the roster, you do wonder if there's a trade in the future, or maybe Cleveland simply slides Joey Cantillo or Slade Cecconi to the bullpen. Nothing wrong with having options. Tanner Bibee might be the guy the Guardians look to deal, though, given his $7.4 million salary that jumps to $10.4 million in 2028 and then $21.4 million. Signing Bubic and now Griffin gives them the depth to do that. -- Schoenfield

Rockies add Peterson, Sandoval to rotation
Peterson's deal: Two years, $32 million

Sandoval's deal: Three years, $42 million

Grade: C

Look, it's not easy being the Colorado Rockies. It's not exactly the place pitchers want to go to extend their careers. But sometimes a player is looking to cash in on what might be his only opportunity at a big payday in free agency, so we get signings like these -- the Rockies desperate for rotation help and signing two left-handers to bigger contracts than anyone would have expected.

Both have had their moments in the big leagues. For Patrick Sandoval, it came with the Angels back in 2022, when he had a 2.91 ERA in 27 starts and allowed just eight home runs in 148 innings. For David Peterson, it come with the New York Mets in 2024, when he went 10-3 with a 2.90 ERA in 21 starts.

But outside of those seasons, neither has provided value that warrants these deals. That one season represents 59% of Sandoval's career value. He has pitched just 149 innings the past three years, missing all of 2025 after Tommy John surgery and posting a 5.12 ERA with the Red Sox in 2026. That one season represents 43% of Peterson's career value. He did at least make 30 starts in 2025 -- the only season either one has pitched the 162 innings needed to qualify for the ERA title.

This completes a rotation makeover for the Rockies after the trade with the White Sox in which they acquired Davis Martin and Luis Castillo. Is it going to turn them into instant playoff contenders? Hardly. In 2026, 213 pitchers threw at least 70 innings. Sandoval ranked 89th in strikeout rate (which is why the Rockies apparently threw $42 million at him); Peterson ranked 126th; Martin ranked 142nd; Castillo ranked 151st.

Really, though, it's not even about building a playoff team. The Rockies just needed live bodies to fill out a rotation that had a 6.28 ERA as a group in 2026. Even for playing half your games in Coors Field, that's beyond abysmal. Indeed, the Rockies tried this route a year ago, signing Michael Lorenzen, Tomoyuki Sugano and Jose Quintana coming off that 119-loss season in 2025. It's safe to say that didn't work out too well: Lorenzen went 3-11 with a 7.08 ERA; Sugano went 12-12 with a 5.37 ERA (which actually translated to 1.8 WAR); and Quintana went 2-3 with a 5.44 ERA and got injured.

Will this new group fare any better? Probably. The best-case scenario is that the Rockies at least get 100 starts out of this new foursome. If that happens, they should avoid 100 losses for the first time since 2022. -- Schoenfield

Tigers secure Gausman on 1-year deal
The deal: One year, $25 million

Grade: B

This signing is a bit of a twist in what has been an inflated market for starting pitchers: Instead of going with a multiyear deal like we've been seeing, the Detroit Tigers have agreed with durable right-hander Kevin Gausman on a one-year contract that will make him the second-highest-paid player on the team behind fellow starter Framber Valdez.

Part of the reasoning for a one-year deal is simply Gausman's age: He's entering his age-36 season. Nonetheless, he has been one of the most reliable starters in the game, second in innings pitched since 2021 and one of just two starters alongside Freddy Peralta to make at least 30 starts each of the past four seasons (and Gausman has done it six straight years). The other reason for the contract length is that Gausman is also coming off his highest ERA during that six-year run, going 9-12 with a 4.51 ERA in 2026 with the Toronto Blue Jays and Chicago Cubs.

In isolation, the deal is fine: It's hard to criticize a one-year contract. While Gausman's ERA was up, there didn't seem to be any decline in his stuff compared with 2025:

2025: 24.4% SO rate, 6.5% BB rate, 26.4% whiff rate, .263 BABIP

2026: 24.5% SO rate, 6.3 BB rate, 23.4% whiff rate, .315 BABIP

OK ... maybe there was a slight decline, as his swing-and-miss rate was down three percentage points and his expected batting average allowed was .250, up from .238 in 2025. All those numbers are down from his 2021-23 peak, but there didn't appear to be much change in his ability from 2025, just a few more home runs allowed and maybe some bad luck on balls in play (and some good luck in 2025).

Gausman was worth 4.0 bWAR in 2025 and 1.1 in 2026; his projection for 2027 probably will split the difference, making him a midrotation starter in a group that will include Valdez, Troy Melton (recently signed to a six-year extension), Keider Montero, River Ryan, Jackson Jobe and the just-signed Luis Gil. That could be an effective group if Melton can extend his breakout (2.76 ERA in 20 starts) to a full season and Ryan, the longtime prospect for the Dodgers obtained in the Tarik Skubal trade, can stay healthy.

In the big picture, though, the Tigers just handed out a combined $30 million for Gausman and Ha-Seong Kim, gambling that both players will be more valuable than they were in 2026. The Tigers are also paying Valdez and Gausman a combined $72.5 million for 2027. Both are durable, and that's a big plus in today's game, but Valdez had a 4.01 ERA last season with a big drop in his strikeout rate. Know anyone Detroit could have spent $72 million on? -- Schoenfield

Royals bag Bohm

The deal: Two years, $20 million

Grade: D

This is the Jonathan India situation all over again, a two-year deal for an average (or worse) player based on ... what? Prospect grade from six years ago?

Alec Bohm solves nothing for the Kansas City Royals and makes the bad trade of Maikel Garcia that much worse. Bohm, assuming the plan is to replace Garcia at third base, is a godawful defender with an offensive profile that suggests 15-20 homers with the K as his home venue and a decent hit tool. He has shown a propensity to punch above his weight in RBI slots, but he'll no longer be doing that while hitting behind Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper and Trea Turner. I've got him projected for just 1.1 WAR despite those bat virtues because of the glove and negative value on the bases. I don't have him any better as an overall player than Nick Loftin, whom he supplants on the depth chart. And as for moving Bohm to the outfield, if that's a thought, forget about it. He can't run and the Royals already have to deal with having Jac Caglianone playing out of position in right.

This move actually drops the Royals' already poor forecast by 0.3 wins in my rough forecast and increases their chances at another last-place finish to more than 64%. Bohm's modest upgrade to the offense is more than offset by his other attributes. The Royals can't afford to misspend money and as with the India fiasco, here they go again. Bohm does fit on some teams. This is not one of them. -- Doolittle

Reds bring back backstop Stephenson
The deal: Three years, $30 million (with opt-out after second year)

Grade: C

Tyler Stephenson has been a fixture behind the plate for the Cincinnati Reds since his rookie season in 2021, a steady if unspectacular presence. The Reds bring him back on a reasonable deal that will keep Stephenson in Cincinnati for at least two more seasons -- keeping the catching position solidified until the team's top prospect, power-hitting Alfredo Duno, is ready to take over.

With Stephenson, you know what you're going to get: He essentially has been a league-average hitter over the past three seasons, maybe a little better going by wRC+ or similar metrics, hitting for some power and drawing enough walks to keep his on-base percentage above water. He's entering his age-30 season, so not a lot should change in his offensive profile in the next two years.

The knock is his defense, where he consistently has ranked near the bottom in Statcast's pitch-framing metric. He ranked 55th out of 56 regular catchers in 2026 at minus-9 runs saved; he ranked 50th out of 57 in 2025; and 45th out of 58 in 2024. Though caught-stealing rates are dependent on both pitcher and catcher, he ranked 64th out of 72 catchers in Statcast's throwing metric in 2026. He does at least rate well in blocking balls in the dirt.

The Reds have a lot of holes to fill or positions to upgrade and it's hard to know how aggressive they're going to be in doing that. So far, the small-market teams have been sitting out free agency, instead waiting for a lockout and whatever labor agreement eventually comes out of it. Re-signing Stephenson doesn't really change much for the Reds, other than offering a small tick up in payroll, since Stephenson made $6.8 million in 2026. It's a fair deal for what he offers, but the Reds still have work do in the outfield and at third base. -- Schoenfield

White Sox mix Taylor into outfield
The deal: Two years, $17 million

Grade: D+

I like Tyrone Taylor as a player. He's a good athlete and defender, even at 33, and has plenty of utility at the plate against left-handed pitchers. The grade is not about him. It's about his fit on the Chicago White Sox, on their payroll, and about what the signing says about how the White Sox see themselves.

Just the other day, Chicago completed a salary-slashing deal that sent trade deadline mistake Luis Castillo to the Rockies. That cleared Castillo's contract from the books but also cost the White Sox the services of right-hander Davis Martin, their longest-tenured player. (Granted, "longest-tenured" is a low bar for the White Sox, who aren't far removed from a full teardown.) Castillo was on the books for $22.8 million in 2027.

That freed up some money that apparently needed to be freed up. Now a third of that in AAV is being earmarked for a 33-year-old fourth outfielder who does not move their projection one iota. He is redundant to Brenton Doyle on the depth chart and if the White Sox needed another righty, there would be a lot more upside to moving one of their young infielders like Caleb Bonemer from another position to fill that limited role. It's just not a great use of resources.

The calculus would be different if Taylor represented some kind of final piece move but he doesn't, and the White Sox shouldn't look at him in that way. They have to recognize they are still a 75-to-77-win team on paper and should still be favoring upside promotions from their system over this kind of investment. The money would have been better used for more pitching. -- Doolittle

After whiffing on Skubal, Jays sign Japan's Taira

The deal: Five years, $80 million

Grade: B+

On one hand, the Toronto Blue Jays' tradition of free agent fallback options continues with the addition of Kaima Taira. On the other hand, if we didn't know anything about Toronto's reported near-miss on Tarik Skubal, there would be no emotional baggage attached to the acquisition of the talented Taira.

While I've touted freshly minted Cub Trevor Rogers as the second-best hurler available in this class, you can make a strong argument that the title should go to Taira. The 5-foot-8 righty's projection is held back some by his history as a reliever, which isn't a bad thing in itself but limits his innings forecast. So too does a track record of iffy control, but that's an area that's been on the upswing for Taira, a trend that arguably got him paid.

The deal itself is fair value if Taira holds down a midrotation spot but turns upside down if he ends up in the bullpen. For now, he slots into the rotation mix along with Dylan Cease, Trey Yesavage and Jose Soriano in Toronto's highly alluring top four. I've got the Jays' starting staff ranked 10th and it would be higher if Toronto's pitching depth outlook was stronger.

Overall, with a solid Louis Varland-led bullpen and top-10 team defense, the Jays are in good shape on the run-prevention side of the ledger, up to eighth in park-neutral runs allowed after this addition. But this is a very unbalanced roster and a power-light offense projects dead last in run scoring. It's the kind of weakness that sinks hopes of contention in the strong AL East.

No problem, right? Go get some power. The market isn't exactly teeming with that quality, so the Blue Jays might have to get creative. Or maybe they're banking on loads of positive regression based on what their offense did the season before last. Even if that's realistic to an extent, from here Toronto needs to redirect whatever remaining resources it was willing to commit to Skubal toward upgrading its offensive profile. -- Doolittle

Detroit gets infield depth in Kim
The deal: One year, $5 million

Grade: C

There are a lot of ways the Detroit Tigers' infield depth chart might break, but here's my read on what is most likely: Ha-Seong Kim will be the every-day shortstop, though Kevin McGonigle is still likely to log time there. McGonigle will get more time at third base, and the presence of Kim is meant to bolster the team defense for one season. At the same time, Kim will serve as a stopgap starter at the position until the Tigers deem prospect Bryce Rainer to be ready, which probably isn't going to be the 2027 season.

It's not splashy, but if moving off shortstop most of the time and focusing on one primary defensive position helps McGonigle stay on a superstar track, $5 million is a bargain no matter what Kim does at the plate, which isn't projected to be much (89 wRC+). Of course, Kim now has easily the lowest durability rating of anyone on the Tigers' defensive array, so he's got to stay on the field for any of this to matter. All in all, if "shrug emoji" were a grade, that's what this one would be. -- Doolittle

Guardians join free agency pitching frenzy, add Bubic
The deal: One year, $17.5 million

Grade: B+

The Cleveland Guardians are getting spendy! The $17.5 million deal they struck with Kris Bubic is a franchise record for a one-year free agent contract and, unofficially, ties the club record for any one-year contract. Francisco Lindor inked an arbitration-fueled deal for the same amount in 2020 that included incentives he did not reach. So, in Cleveland, Bubic equals Lindor.

In all seriousness, I'm a big Bubic guy who once touted him as a Cy Young contender, and I did so before his 2025 breakout season. He was on track to earn some Cy Young votes that year, too, before his season was clipped due to one of a string of injuries with which he's had to deal with over the past few seasons. Hence the one-year contract, one that Bubic has to be looking at as a make-good opportunity with a team that has a proven track record with hurlers.

It's a win-win for both sides. Bubic gets a handsome one-year payout and, with a healthy platform season, would be in line to earn much more next year. The Guardians get a versatile lefty who could hold down a rotation spot all year, or become a valuable multi-inning option in the always-potent Cleveland bullpen. The salary, one year or not, suggests the Guardians have the rotation option at the top of their list.

It's a good signing with limited risk. And it's a deal any number of Cleveland competitors may wish they'd struck. The Guardians were already my very early favorites to repeat in the AL Central, and the addition of Bubic only bolsters that status. -- Doolittle

Orioles make big rotation splash with Peralta
The deal: Five years, $125 million

Grade: C+

Following reports that Trevor Rogers was heading to the Chicago Cubs, the Baltimore Orioles replaced Rogers in their rotation with Freddy Peralta, agreeing to a similar five-year, $125 million deal. In these final days before the lockout, pitchers are getting paid: Peralta's deal exceeded the prediction of four years and $96 million with an additional year and a higher average salary. It's the third largest free agent contract in Orioles history, behind the infamous Chris Davis disaster and last year's $155 deal with Pete Alonso.

In one sense, the Orioles come out ahead: They'll receive draft pick compensation for losing Rogers but won't have to give up anything for signing Peralta, since he was traded in the middle of his walk year. Otherwise though, I prefer Rogers, who is two years younger, has less mileage on his arm and appears to be hitting his peak as a pitcher.

That's not a knock on Fastball Freddy: He's been a reliable and productive starter going back to his breakout with the Milwaukee Brewers in 2021 and is riding a streak of four consecutive seasons with 30-plus starts. He and Kevin Gausman are the only pitchers to do that each of the past four years, so the health record is important -- especially for an Orioles organization that has had trouble keeping pitchers on the mound. Still, they're paying for Peralta's age 31-to-35 seasons coming off a 2026 season that saw a precipitous decline in his strikeout rate.

Peralta's best season came with the Brewers in 2025, when he went 17-6 with a 2.70 ERA. Some will see that as his upside, but that was clearly an outlier, driven by a low average allowed on balls in play. Since 2023, his ERAs have been 3.86, 3.68, 2.70 and 4.42, respectively. He struggled with the New York Mets in the first half of 2026 (4.99 ERA) and much was made on how the Tampa Bay Rays "fixed" him after they acquired him, most notably eliminating his windup, changing his position on the rubber and using his changeup more often.

Maybe those adjustments will lead to a new and better Peralta. Over his final 10 appearances with the Rays, including the postseason, he had a 1.82 ERA. But his strikeout rate was just 19.5%, well below his career average of 28.6% and below even what he did with the Mets (22.1%). The big change, really, was simply walking fewer batters -- and maybe having some of that good Tampa Bay defense behind him.

Indeed, that's the biggest concern for these next five years: Peralta has made a living off that four-seamer at the top of the zone, but while he's still maintaining 94-mph velocity, it's become a little less dominant through the years, with a whiff rate that was 29.2% in 2023 down to 22.4% in 2026. What's interesting about his time with the Rays is that he also threw that fastball more often -- 60% of the time, compared to historical rates of 53% or so. He threw his fastball/changeup in more than 86% of his pitches, so he became much more of a two-pitch pitcher.

It will be fascinating to see if this is the new Peralta moving forward. The Orioles ranked 17th in rotation ERA, but this is basically an even swap of Rogers for Peralta, which won't change the projection for the club. Barring another signing, Baltimore will need some of the young starters to step up behind Peralta, Kyle Bradish, Shane Baz and Brandon Young, who are the current top four. -- Schoenfield

Cubs add two-time Japanese MVP Sato

The deal: Six years, $120 million

Grade: B-

At the very bottom of the analysis I did on the Mets' Tarik Skubal deal, there's a chart that shows how teams have improved or gotten worse since the start of the offseason. The baseline to make that comparison is an estimate of how teams would project if they were bringing back the same collection of talent in the organization with which they ended the 2026 season. The Mets, the subject of the analysis, were all the way on the left as the most improved. All the way to the right: the Cubs.

That was entirely a function of the number of key Chicago players who hit free agency. With the roster hollowed out by these departures, the Cubs had as many holes to fill as any club. But they also had the most spending capacity, which is a factor in the up-to-date projection but only goes so far because we don't really know how those holes will be filled. Over the past 15 hours or so, we have a much better idea of that after the Cubs have landed the top remaining free agent pitcher (by my rankings) in Trevor Rogers and the top available power bat in Teruaki Sato.

As much attention as the Cubs' rotation shortage has gotten, Chicago also entered the hot stove season looking at having to replace incumbent corner outfielders Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki. More than the positional need though was the need for more raw power, a collective skill at which I had the Cubs ranked 18th. Sato bumps that up to 15th and their park-neutral run projection climbs from 724 to 737. Chicago's win projection climbs accordingly: the Cubs are up to an 85.7 win forecast, and while they are still looking up at the Brewers in the NL Central, their playoff probability has now jumped from 53% to 58%.

Sato's power is legit, but there are real concerns about overly-aggressive approach in his profile, which is always worrying for a player making the jump from overseas to the majors. He's also a lefty swinger, and while his platoon splits in Japan were mild, he'll still have to prove himself as an every-day hitter in the majors. One non-severe concern for me is defense. With no room for him at third base in Chicago, he's slated for one of the open corner outfield slots. He has the arm to carry right field, if that's the plan. He's an average runner though, and these days, speed is the name of the game when it comes to a standout outfield defense.

Still, Pete Crow-Armstrong's range should mitigate much of that, and if the Cubs come up with a solid defender for the other outfield spot, they should be fine, which in Chicago's case means remaining near the top of the majors in the fielding department. The aggressive approach creates risk, but the upside of lefty-side homers is worth it. If Sato adapts well to playing in the grass every day, it should work out fine. -- Doolittle

Cubs begin rotation overhaul with Rogers
The deal: Five years, $120 million

Grade: B

One starter down, three to go? Signing left-hander Trevor Rogers is just the first move the Chicago Cubs will need to fix a rotation that ranked 18th in ERA in 2026 and, more importantly, has Clay Holmes, Shota Imanaga, Matthew Boyd, Kevin Gausman and David Peterson all in free agency, with Cade Horton, Justin Steele and Ben Brown all recovering from injuries.

Edward Cabrera was the only potential starter still on the roster and healthy at the end of 2026 -- and he was pitching out of the bullpen after battling injuries and posting a 5.96 ERA. Horton won't return until late in the season after Tommy John surgery, Steele was at least rehabbing at the end of the season and Brown had cervical spine surgery early in November. Those three have to be considered unknown quantities at this point.

That's a lot of uncertainty. Enter Rogers, who becomes the No. 1 starter by default. While the contract will include deferrals that will lower the present value, it's still a huge deal to give for a pitcher who has qualified for the ERA title just once in six seasons and is coming off a 4.03 ERA with Baltimore.

Rogers ranked as the No. 5 starter on Kiley McDaniel's top 50 free agents, with a projected four-year, $76 million contract, so while the raw value is $24 million per season, the deferrals will bring it closer to the $19 million average ESPN predicted, with an extra season tacked on.

Nobody questions Rogers' upside -- best on display in 2025, when he had 1.81 ERA in 18 starts with the Orioles, and then with a 2.90 ERA over his final 20 starts in 2026. He works with a 93-95 mph four-seamer up in the zone that generates enough swing and miss -- 24.7%, which ranked 33rd out of 140 pitchers with at least 100 innings -- and held batters to a .227 average. His sweeper is his most effective pitch, and he uses that to dominate left-handed batters. He also mixes in a sinker, cutter and changeup (his second-most utilized pitch, but batters hit .336 off it in 2026).

Rogers walked just 39 batters in 30 starts, and going to the Cubs, with their stellar defense, should help lower opponents' batting average on balls in play. He'll need to get his changeup back, since he needs that to help counter right-handed batters, who hit .269 with 18 of the 19 home runs he allowed. That's something to watch: His fly ball rate went up last season, and the ball was flying out of Wrigley in 2026, when it was one of the more homer-friendly parks in the majors.

Due to his injury history, Rogers doesn't have a lot of mileage on his arm and maybe that's a good thing -- 689 innings in the majors compared to, say, Freddy Peralta, a pitcher who might end up with a similar contract, who is two years older and has thrown 1,100 innings. That's the biggest issue here: his durability. Rogers missed time in 2022 with back spasms, made just four starts in 2023 with a biceps issue, dislocated his right kneecap in the offseason which delayed the start to his 2025 season, and even missed two weeks with an illness early this past season, which might have contributed to his slow start.

Still, I like the pitcher and the stuff and won't be surprised if he ends up making a couple of All-Star Games with the Cubs over the next five years. -- Schoenfield

Mets get help at first base with Goldschmidt
The deal: One year, $8 million

Grade: B

As Paul Goldschmidt has aged out of his peak seasons that culminated with the 2022 National League MVP Award, he has continued to do one thing exceptionally well: mash left-handers. Over the past two seasons, he has hit .317/.402/.572 against lefties -- the fifth-highest OPS among all hitters (Aaron Judge, Shea Langeliers, Coby Mayo and Jackson Chourio are ahead of him, in case you're curious).

Against left-handers, he strikes out just 14.8% of the time, but he hasn't sacrificed power, hitting 18 home runs in 306 at-bats. Against right-handers, however, he has been useless, putting up backup infielder numbers: .235/.271/.337 with 10 home runs in 528 at-bats. The Yankees gave him nearly 200 plate appearances against righties in 2026 for some reason, but Goldschmidt should be strictly viewed as a platoon bat at first base or DH.

Certainly, the Mets needed help at first base and/or DH: They were 28th in OPS at first base and 20th at DH. Between the two positions combined, the Mets were 29th in OPS, 29th in RBIs, 29th in batting average and 29th in on-base percentage. Goldschmidt should help, even in his age-39 season, but he's only one-fourth of the equation.

The problem here is it's hard to carry that kind of player with modern roster-building, when the four bench players will have to include a catcher, infielder and outfielder. The Mets are already rostering Mark Vientos, Jorge Polanco and Jared Young, all of whom shouldn't play any position other than first base. Brett Baty is around as a multiposition backup and Bo Bichette can serve as the emergency backup to Francisco Lindor at shortstop, so maybe there is enough versatility here.

Perhaps the best option will be playing Baty more in the outfield with Juan Soto getting regular DH time, and Goldschmidt then platooning with Polanco or Young at first base. If Polanco can find his 2025 stroke, that could work, and Young was at least not terrible (and he has torn up Triple-A for years, so maybe he can be moderately productive). Goldschmidt fills a role, but the real keys to a better offense for the Mets will be a healthier Soto and Lindor plus a much better Bichette (not to mention Carson Benge and A.J. Ewing improving in their sophomore seasons). If all that happens, this could end up being a dynamic lineup. -- Schoenfield

Big Apple blockbuster! Mets, Skubal agree to record deal

The deal: Nine years, $450 million

Grade: B+

It's not often that a two-time Cy Young winner still in his prime and regarded as one of the best starting pitchers in the game becomes available in free agency. These are potential franchise-altering difference-makers, maybe a final piece needed to build a World Series champion. If you have an owner who wants to win and is willing to spend the money, you make it happen at any cost.

Read the full grade here.

Yankees reinforce bullpen with Bednar, Loaisiga
The deals: David Bednar accepts one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer; Jonathan Loáisiga agrees to two-year, $18 million deal

Grade: C+

Let's combine these two moves into one overall grade as the Yankees piece together the back end of their bullpen -- a pen that ranked second in the majors with a 3.13 ERA in 2026. The Yankees shoved Bednar into a corner by giving him a qualifying offer, which promised to limit his demand in free agency since he would have been tied to draft pick compensation. By accepting it, Bednar's salary is now the highest average salary for a reliever, topping Edwin Diaz's $23 million with the Dodgers.

Other than a blip in 2024, Bednar has been steady since 2021, first with the Pirates and then with the Yankees after coming over at the trade deadline in 2025, posting sub-3.00 ERAs in five of his six seasons, including 2.47 ERA in 2026 when he racked up 35 saves in 39 opportunities. He throws a four-seamer, splitter and curveball, with his splitter his big out pitch, holding batters to a .149 average in 2026 and .175 in 2025, with just one home run over the two seasons. His four-seamer can be more hittable, although he kept it in the park this past season. The Yankees love his toughness and showed their high regard for him in giving him the qualifying offer. He's not an A-plus closer, but he's very good and a safe bet on a one-year -- albeit expensive -- deal.

Loáisiga, meanwhile, returns to the club where he pitched from 2018 to 2025 -- although "pitched" is a loose description since he was often injured. In his one year with Arizona, he posted a 2.42 ERA across 67 innings, just the second time he's surpassed 50 innings. He still has an electric 98 mph sinker, although he fanned just 48 batters. Even for a sinker-reliant pitcher, that's a low total, although he did produce a high ground ball rate and a lot of soft contact. We'll see how that works without Geraldo Perdomo and Nolan Arenado behind him.

The problem is the durability history, and Loáisiga is replacing free agent Paul Blackburn, who had an amazing year, with a 1.59 ERA in 85 innings. Loáisiga isn't going to match that ERA or throw that many innings -- but Blackburn was unlikely to do that again, either. Overall, the Yankees have at least locked in their closer and top right-handed setup guy, although they are paying a steep price at $32 million to do it. -- Schoenfield

Rockies add pair of starters in deal with White Sox

Colorado Rockies get:

RHP Davis Martin

RHP Luis Castillo

Chicago White Sox get:

LHP Sean Sullivan

C Douglas Veliz

White Sox grade: C+

The White Sox appear to be spending proverbial money to spend proverbial money. That is to say, they are moving past the Castillo mistake from the last trade deadline -- one whose ramifications were primarily monetary -- and to do it, they are folding in a legitimate starter in Martin -- a pitcher who, for the first few weeks of the 2026 season, looked like a Cy Young candidate. They aren't spending actual money but are rearranging resources in hopes of spending money in a more productive way.

That's just reality, not an attempt to overhype Martin, whose season came unraveled the deeper we got into the calendar and who was ultimately not in position to help Chicago's staff once it reached the postseason. Still, he put up more than 140 innings in each of the past two seasons with a 104 ERA+ during the pre-arbitration phase of his service time window. He was a valuable player for Chicago and therefore is now that for Colorado.

This perspective speaks to how badly the White Sox wanted to clear Castillo off their books, and his departure -- which rids them of a $22.75 million 2027 salary plus a semi-unlikely vesting option for 2028 -- opens up the payroll so that Chicago can further upgrade a rotation it thinks it upgraded with the signing of Dustin May earlier this week.

Castillo was ghastly -- harsh as that sounds -- last season for the Mariners before Chicago acquired him at the trade deadline, and he was even worse after the deal. It was the first truly bad season of his mostly very good 10-year big league career, but it felt like it was one that was a result of trends that were years in the making. The one and truly virtuous aspect of this deal for the White Sox is that it rids them of the considerable risk that Castillo bounces back and justifies his sizable salary.

Sullivan is a long, lean lefty with so-so stuff who relies on deception -- perhaps not the soft-tossing lefty of yore, but someone along those lines. Veliz is a 17-year-old catcher who originally was signed for $50,000 out of Venezuela. Maybe someday you'll read his name again.

Chicago's grade is entirely provisional. The White Sox have opened up payroll space that needs to be parlayed into a meaningful upgrade. The 2027 rotation, once it's in place, will have some kind of configuration that includes May, an unsigned pitcher to be named and the other returnees to the staff. The gamble is that this new group will be better than simply running it back with Castillo while hoping for more consistency from Martin.

Right now, it's hard to say which path would have been better.

Rockies grade: B

I mean, why not? It's easy to make the crude argument against Castillo -- over 126 games for the Mariners, he went 43-40 with a 3.69 ERA while pitching half the time in one of baseball's most pitcher-friendly contexts. (During those seasons, his ERA was 3.07 at T-Mobile Park and 4.38 on the road.) Now he's headed to the wood-chipper of a pitching context at Coors Field and doing so at the nadir of his career.

Still, for the Rockies, it's a worthy gamble especially since it lands them Martin in the process. Is Martin the right pitcher for Coors Field? Who knows? But the still-new brain trust in Colorado needs to show it has real ideas about who will and who will not be able to function from the pitcher's mound in the Rockies' home venue.

Martin has real remaining upside, but Castillo is really the intriguing part here because he's a veteran with a lot to prove given the lack of long-term certainty around his contract status. Maybe he's done. Fine. It's only money, right? And you've still got Martin. But if Castillo flourishes by whatever definition that means when pitching in Coors, it's more than a productive performance for a team likely to land once again in the NL West cellar. It's a proof of concept. The Rockies need all of those they can get. -- Doolittle

Twins bring Gray back to Minnesota
The deal: Two years, $55 million

Grade: B+

Sonny Gray had one of the best seasons of his career with the Minnesota Twins back in 2023, when he made 32 starts, posted a 2.79 ERA and a 5.6 WAR, and finished second in the Cy Young Award voting. (He won just eight games, plagued by a lack of run support and a poor bullpen.) The Twins are hoping for a happy reunion, signing Gray to the largest total value free agent pitcher contract in franchise history (tied with a four-year deal for Ervin Santana back in 2015). The second year is a player option, so this could end up being a one-year deal.

This wasn't necessarily where everyone expected Gray to land, especially coming off a strong season with the Boston Red Sox. He finished 18-5, tied with Cristopher Sanchez for the major league lead in wins, while posting a 2.72 ERA, good for eighth in the majors. While Gray had some injuries earlier in his career, he has been durable across the past four seasons, averaging 30 starts and 175 innings. That almost makes him Old Hoss Radbourn in today's game. While Gray's ERA has jumped all over the place, his FIP (fielding independent pitching) speaks to more consistency, with marks of 3.40, 2.83, 3.12, 3.39 and 3.47 going back to 2022.

The negatives: Gray is 37 years old and his strikeout rate took a big dip in 2026, dropping from 28.4% over the previous two seasons to 21.8%. That's still playable -- the MLB average for starting pitchers was 21.9% -- but it's something to watch. However, he's such a smart pitcher -- mixing in six different pitches with excellent command -- that he can succeed even with a lower K rate.

It's a nice move for the Twins, who ranked 22nd in rotation ERA this past season. They've indicated an intent to keep Joe Ryan. Plus, Pablo Lopez is aiming to be ready by Opening Day in his return from Tommy John surgery, so Minnesota could roll out a rotation of Gray, Ryan, Lopez, Taj Bradley (their top starter in 2026 with 4.4 WAR) and Bailey Ober, with Dean Kremer, Connor Prielipp and Zebby Matthews as depth. Ryan, Lopez, Ober and Kremer are all in the final years of their deals, so there are trade possibilities here, especially since Minnesota needs to improve the bullpen.

Gray's contract projection was for two years and $42 million, so the deal comes in higher than that; this might be par for the course for starting pitchers given Dustin May's inflated three-year, $52.5 million deal with the Chicago White Sox. In one sense, the best-case scenario for the Twins is if Gray has another good season and he opts out. If he does have a good season and Lopez bounces back, this has a chance to be a really nice rotation, with Prielipp having breakout potential in his second year. And a good rotation in the American League Central will make the Twins contenders. -- Schoenfield

Mariners add Garcia to infield in six-player swap

Seattle Mariners get:

IF Maikel Garcia

RHP James McArthur

RHP L.P. Langevin

Kansas City Royals get:

RHP Bryce Miller

RHP Logan Evans

LHP Jose Ferrer

Mariners grade: A-

Garcia is the best player in the deal, and the difference is enough to make this a slam dunk win for Seattle. Nagging injuries undermined Garcia's 2026 season after his breakout the year before; but even so, his contract and patience at the plate remained well above average, and he was still one of baseball's top defensive third basemen. While the injuries cost him in the power department and on the bases, Garcia is entering his age-27 season as a good bet to bounce back to All-Star form. His well-documented penchant for self-improvement also supports the argument for positive regression.

Under contract through 2031 on team-friendly terms, Garcia is a major upgrade at a soft spot on the Mariners' depth chart. Seattle's defensive projection at the hot corner leaped from 21st to first in my system, and the offensive leap in runs from that spot was about 10 spots, to No. 12. Garcia's range will only help the overall infield defense, as he will team with Colt Emerson, Cole Young and Josh Naylor to give Seattle a pretty dynamic group.

The Mariners had the kind of surplus on their organizational rotation chart to easily absorb the loss of Miller. Similar to last year, they look a little thin in bullpen lefties, but Ferrer didn't prove to be the splash addition in that role Seattle hoped for anyway. McArthur is a sneaky get here. He hasn't pitched in the majors since 2024 because of injury but was closing games for the Royals before getting hurt. He's a worthy flier. Langevin is a lower-level prospect, a righty with big strikeout rates and shaky command.

The Mariners' right-now win projection climbs over 90 with this trade, and at 67% division title odds, Seattle is a heavy early favorite in a soft division. This trade only bolsters the chances that the Mariners bounce back in 2027 to become the team we thought they were in 2026.

Royals grade: C-

The Royals just don't have the kind of organizational depth to be trading one of their few difference-makers for a package of pitchers who in total upgrade their staff only marginally and offer little collective upside. In the near term, the trade makes the Royals worse, and the problems only compound from here given that they had Garcia under team control for so long.

Miller moves right into a middle-of-the-rotation slot for the Royals, and if Michael Wacha declines, it's possible Miller will be Kansas City's top starter next season. Still, Miller, 27, has a career ERA+ of 95 and is at 80 over the past two seasons, both of which have been undermined by injury. For the Royals, the hope would be that Miller is ready to take the kind of leap that Wacha and Seth Lugo did when they joined the Royals. And to be fair, Miller's Statcast metrics definitely suggest that could happen.

Ferrer, as mentioned, had a poor season in Seattle after being acquired for catcher Harry Ford. Ferrer has a career OPS+ of 96 but still becomes the Royals' top bullpen lefty, almost by default. Evans was a ranked organizational prospect in Seattle and had a decent debut season in 2025. He underwent Tommy John surgery, the internal brace version, in January. He projected with mid- to lower-rotation upside before getting hurt.

The instant change in the Royals' projection kind of tells the story. The new pitchers are pushing not-great pitchers down the depth chart, so Kansas City's profile improves by about 16 runs on the prevention side. Garcia's defensive loss is fairly marginal for Kansas City, as Nick Loftin is a good defender, as well. But the loss of the bat is about a 17-run hit for the Royals' run production.

The end result? The same amount of bad, just shaped differently. The Royals should have received more for a player of Garcia's ability and contract. -- Doolittle

White Sox add midrotation piece with May
The deal: Three years, $52.5 million

Grade: D+

We've had two significant signings off the free agent market so far, and both involve freshly minted ex-Milwaukee Brewers: After Jake Bauers landed with the Boston Red Sox on Friday, the Chicago White Sox plucked Dustin May off the championship Milwaukee pitching staff.

Whereas Boston was banking on Bauers' 2026 breakout being his current true talent level, the White Sox are perhaps taking a bigger gamble that May's past five years do not represent his real level of ability. Since his early shine as a top Los Angeles Dodgers prospect, which included some promising early work in the majors, May's career has been journeyman-like. Around injuries that cost him the 2024 season, he has put up 0.9 bWAR with a 91 ERA+ over 356 big-league innings for the period covering 2022 through last season.

May became a fallback addition for the Brewers at the 2026 trade deadline after more glitzy pursuits (ahem, Tarik Skubal) fell short. May put up a 106 ERA+ for the St. Louis Cardinals before the trade and, given the Brewers' track record with acquired pitchers, you had to figure the move boded well for an even better post-trade performance. But that's not what happened. May had a 5.65 ERA and 75 ERA+ over 10 starts for the Brewers and was not a core part of Milwaukee's postseason rotation.

This uninspiring platform performance partially explains the grade above, but only partially. We'll see how things shake out in the market when we have more signings to work from -- May is the first pitcher to land a sizable deal -- but this seems like an overpay at least in terms of years. ESPN's Kiley McDaniel projected a one-year, $14 million deal for May, while a consensus projection from various outlets looked something more like two years, $24.7 million.

The White Sox are likely banking on May's tantalizing tracking data, which in 2026 had him in the 85th percentile in fastball velocity (average of 96.8 mph) and 72nd percentile in extension. Indeed, my own projection model sees enough in May keeping his value that it suggested a three-year, $45.9 million deal would be justified, which at least is in the neighborhood of what he got from the White Sox.

As it stands, May slots in behind Grant Taylor in the revamped Chicago rotation, just ahead of Sean Burke and Luis Castillo. Ah, Castillo: Is he a cautionary tale for a White Sox approach that liked him, as it likes May, despite underwhelming results before the deal? We'll see. May is also pushing pitchers such as David Sandlin and Davis Martin down in the pecking order, though there's no guarantee he's going to be that much better than them, if at all. I've got May adding 0.9 wins to Chicago's right-now roster, which pushes its 2027 playoff odds up by about three percentage points.

That's fairly marginal when you remember that the White Sox were overachievers in 2026. It was a great story, but it also means their starting baseline is somewhere south of the 84 games they won in 2026. If they are really looking to bolster their chances heading into 2027 -- and beyond -- then opportunity cost comes into play even though the White Sox should have some remaining spending capacity, or at least you would hope so. Would a little patience have netted them someone like Sonny Gray, Michael King or Freddy Peralta?

If the White Sox still go after someone like that and the May signing doesn't end up as their one big rotation splash, then maybe we push that grade up to the C-minus range. Given what we know at the moment, though, I'm underwhelmed. -- Doolittle

Red Sox get offensive boost with Bauers addition

The deal: Four years, $58 million

Grade: A

The Red Sox weren't high on anybody's list of teams likely to sign Jake Bauers given they already have an All-Star first baseman in Willson Contreras, but this signing is an early candidate for best move of the offseason. The grade reflects two thoughts: (1) that Bauers' breakout -- he finished 11th in the majors in OPS and third in on-base percentage this past season -- is for real; and (2) that the contract is a steal at $14.5 million per year.

Bauers will be entering his age-31 season, and, of course, spent years struggling in the majors before finally figuring things out, so while there would generally be concern that his 2026 season was a fluke, all the advanced metrics suggest the opposite. His Statcast numbers: 93rd percentile bat speed, 94th percentile hard-hit rate, 93rd percentile chase rate, 98th percentile walk rate. Those are real skills that aren't going to diminish overnight and should allow him to remain a productive hitter (he even hit left-handers well, so should project as a full-time player). Everyone saw the quality of his at-bats during the postseason throughout the Milwaukee Brewers' title run; he was named MVP of the National League Championship Series.

As for the contract, compare it to Josh Naylor's deal last year, when he signed a five-year, $92.5 million contract with the Seattle Mariners. Naylor was two years younger, but he was coming off a 129-OPS+, 3.0-WAR season compared with Bauers' 140 OPS+ and 3.3 WAR. Yes, Naylor had the longer track record of success but less power and a lower OBP. Signing Bauers for $58 million looks like a potential bargain.

Contreras is under contract for 2027 with a team option for 2028 and is the better fielder, so Bauers slots in as the DH. That leaves Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu in the outfield. Masataka Yoshida is still around for one more year as a backup, and the Red Sox will likely look to trade Jarren Duran, who still has two years of team control but is estimated to make $11.1 million in arbitration. With Duran coming off a bad season at the plate, the Red Sox might non-tender him if they can't trade him.

No doubt there will be criticism that the Red Sox needed a right-handed batter instead, but they actually had a slightly higher OPS against left-handers (.734 to .710). They just needed a good hitter, regardless of which side of the plate he stands on.

Remember that they also acquired the right-handed Curtis Mead from the Washington Nationals only to see him get injured in his first game with them. He'll be back and should slot in at second base. Boston also has shortstop Franklin Arias, one of the top three or four prospects in the minors who demolished Double- and Triple-A this year. Indeed, if Bauers comes close to his 2026 numbers and Anthony hits like everyone thought he was going to in 2026, this could be one of the best lineups in the league:

LF Anthony (L)

RF Abreu (L)

1B Contreras (R)

DH Bauers (L)

CF Rafaela (R)

2B Mead (R)

C Adley Rutschman (S)

SS Arias (R) / Trevor Story (R)

3B Caleb Durbin (R)

As for the Brewers, it's sad to see a postseason hero go, although not necessarily unexpected. They could have afforded this contract, but they have first-base prospects just about ready in Andrew Fischer, who led the minors with 48 home runs, and Blake Burke, who hit 34 home runs and stole 29 bases. They also have Andrew Vaughn on hand as a placeholder if Fischer and Burke aren't ready. Plus, they might need this money to sign William Contreras to a long-term extension. The Brewers will be fine. -- Schoenfield

Braves bolster bullpen by landing Phillips
The deal: Three years, $35 million

Grade: B-

The Atlanta Braves don't go after the biggest free agents -- B.J. Upton's $75 million deal in 2013 remains the largest free agent contract in franchise history -- but president of baseball operations Alex Anthopoulos does like to strike as early as possible in the offseason, and he did that again with Evan Phillips.

Phillips will essentially take the roster spot of Raisel Iglesias, so the Braves will get a little younger and maybe a little better, although Iglesias had a good season as the closer in 2026 following some bumps in 2025. The Braves had one of the best bullpens in the majors this past year, leading in win probability added while ranking fourth in ERA and sixth in OPS allowed. Iglesias departs as a free agent, but Didier Fuentes or Robert Suarez can replace him as the ninth-inning guy, with Phillips likely slotting in as a setup man alongside lefties Dylan Lee and Dylan Dodd.

Phillips was one of the best relievers in the majors with the Dodgers in 2022-23 before suffering shoulder and elbow injuries at the end of the 2024 season and finally undergoing Tommy John surgery in June 2025. He returned to make 31 appearances with the Dodgers in 2026, finishing with 33 strikeouts and just six walks in 26 innings. The stuff looked good -- he was throwing a little harder than pre-injury -- although he did serve up five home runs, and his injury history makes a three-year deal a little risky.

The belief was that the Braves' pitching priority this offseason would be a starter, but signing Phillips will allow them to stretch out Fuentes as a starter in spring training. He does have a three-pitch arsenal in his fastball, slider and splitter, and he has thrown a curveball in the past, so as effective as Fuentes was in relief as a rookie in 2026, it makes sense to see if it can work out for him in the rotation. -- Schoenfield

Tigers kick off free agency with Pagan deal
The deal: One year, $11.5 million

Grade: C

A key reason the Detroit Tigers finished 76-86 despite a plus-71 run differential was the bullpen: Despite finishing 12th in ERA, it ranked 26th in win probability added, so it performed worse in high-leverage situations. Out with Kenley Jansen, in with Emilio Pagan, who has been the Reds' closer the past two seasons.

Jansen was only 22-for-28 in saves in 2026, so maybe Pagan is only a small upgrade, but like Jansen, Pagan has been prone to the home run, serving up 17 in 111⅓ innings over the past two seasons. The Tigers are betting that getting out of Cincinnati -- where he allowed 12 of those 17 home runs -- will help. Pagan is a three-pitch reliever, with a splitter that he throws primarily to left-handers and a cutter he throws to right-handers. But his 95 mph fastball is rather pedestrian for a modern closer, and batters have hit 12 home runs off it the past two seasons.

Pagan is also turning 36 years old and his fastball velo dropped from 95.8 mph in 2025 to 94.9 in 2026, so there are a couple of red flags here. The Tigers had to add somebody to the bullpen, and doing so before the anticipated lockout is logical, but Pagan projects as a midtier closer rather than the elite guy Detroit needs. Kyle Finnegan and Will Vest both struggled in 2026, so the Tigers could still nab a reliable right-handed setup guy. -- Schoenfield

stories.headline: Liverpool are all smiles as Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak start to click
stories.summary: Another match, another fine set of displays from Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak. Is the huge investment in Liverpool's forward line beginning to pay off?
stories.body:
BRUGES, Belgium -- Florian Wirtz was bemused by the question. When it was put to the Liverpool midfielder this week that he has seemingly rediscovered his smile of late, he was quick to set the record straight.

"I've heard a lot of people talking about my smiling or if I don't smile that much, maybe that's only because the people don't really know me," he said in a news conference ahead of Liverpool's UEFA Champions League clash with Club Brugge. "Normally I'm a very positive guy ... I'm just trying to play football -- that's my job and that's what I'm trying to do."

Certainly, after scoring in a fifth consecutive game for club and country in the Reds' 3-0 victory over Brugge on Wednesday, Wirtz can consider it a job well done. The 23-year-old has been under a microscope since his £116 million move from Bayer Leverkusen in the summer of 2025, with every facet of every underwhelming performance forensically dissected.

His record in Germany -- where he registered 53 goals and 59 assists in 186 appearances for Leverkusen -- suggested he would be an instant hit at Anfield. But, after a disappointing debut campaign, Wirtz's slow-burn start to his second season has now well and truly burst into life.

After providing an assist and a spectacular goal in Liverpool's 4-0 demolition of Manchester United on Sunday, Wirtz added another fine finish to his collection against Brugge when he beat Yann Sommer at his near post with a curling effort from the edge of the box. If he can carry his rich vein of form into this weekend's Merseyside derby against Everton, Liverpool fans might consider a chunk of his eye-watering transfer fee already repaid.

It was fitting, too, that it was Alexander Isak who bookended the scoring against Brugge. Like Wirtz, the Sweden international had been touted externally as an anticlimactic addition to the Liverpool squad during a debut campaign in which both form and fitness proved problematic.

After combining for just 19 goal contributions in 71 appearances last season, Isak and Wirtz have already managed 20 in 33 appearances this term.

With a goal in either half against Brugge, Isak now has 10 goals for the season in all competitions and has become just the eighth player in Liverpool's history to score in six consecutive away games. His first was a trademark finish from close range after an error from Sommer opened the door for Dominik Szoboszlai to lay the ball off in the 18-yard box.

His second -- a lovely dinked finish over the goalkeeper after a long ball from Alisson Becker -- was that of a striker brimming with confidence, while his work rate and link-up play proved instrumental in downing a Brugge side who were 11 games unbeaten going into Wednesday's match.

"It's always difficult to say exactly where you are and how good you are, but I can say I'm in a good place and the team is in a good place, most importantly," Isak told TNT Sports post-match. "Hopefully, it gets better from here.

"The attack in general is beginning to click. We have a lot of different combinations and whoever comes in, we have a dangerous attack. It feels good."

It was a sentiment shared by Iraola, who will know the trajectory of his team's season depends heavily on whether Wirtz and Isak can maintain their current form.

"Both are now in a good place," the Liverpool boss said in his post-match news conference. "When the team overall is playing well and we are getting good results, everyone looks a little better. When everything collectively is not there, everyone looks a little bit worse.

"The important part is they help the team to play well, to win games, to get results and if we play well then we have chances, we are solid, everyone will play their part and will look better. Alex and Flo right now are in a good moment."

Indeed, Liverpool as a collective find themselves in a good spot under Iraola. They are the first team in 38 games to keep a clean sheet against a free-scoring Brugge side and have moved up to fifth in the Champions League league phase table.

Having won four of their five games in the competition so far this term, they remain on course for a third consecutive finish in the top eight.

While Liverpool are still far from the finished article, there positive signs are beginning to emerge all over the pitch. Goalkeeper Alisson once again showed his class with a fine save from Felix Lemarechal, while teenager Rio Ngumoha sparkled after replacing the injured Víctor Muñoz in the first half.

The withdrawal of the Spain international after he sustained a heavy knock to his knee was the one blemish on an otherwise perfect night for Liverpool -- although Iraola said Muñoz was "optimistic" when he spoke with him after the game.

"I am very pleased with the result and the performance overall," Iraola said. "The result, 3-0, you can think it was an easy game but I don't think it was.

"We were facing a very good team that was tied with us [in the table] in the Champions League, having an incredible run of games and scoring loads of goals. I value a lot the clean sheet and the win."

As for Wirtz, his tally of eight goal contributions in his last five games for club and country suggests the tide may finally be starting to turn in his favour. Forget his smile, the midfielder now looks to have found his feet at Anfield and Liverpool are, at long last, reaping the rewards.

stories.headline: Luis Suárez says 'no excuses left' as Miami looks to avoid early playoff exit
stories.summary: Luis Suárez said there are "no excuses left" for Inter Miami as the defending MLS Cup champion stares at a possible first-round playoff exit.
stories.body:
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. -- Luis Suárez said there are "no excuses left" for Inter Miami as the defending MLS Cup champion stares at a possible first-round elimination from this year's MLS playoffs.

Miami lost 3-0 to the Columbus Crew in the first game of the round one best-of-three series at home on Saturday. Suárez and Co. must now win Game 2 on Friday to ensure a decisive third game back in Miami and avoid immediate elimination.

"It's clear that at a club like this, we have an obligation to win, getting eliminated on Friday would be a disappointment, and that's how we should see it," Suárez said on Wednesday.

"There are no excuses left, not the pitch, not fatigue, nothing. It's time to face reality. If we do get knocked out, we'll be the first to be self-critical. But let's hope that doesn't happen, because we are the ones primarily responsible, we're the ones out there on the pitch.

"The coach can provide the tools, but the decisions and the actions on the field are entirely up to us. Every single player needs to take that responsibility. Everyone knows what they can contribute this Friday; we need 150%, even 200%, from every one of us to bring this series back home."

Seeded second in the Eastern Conference after a rollercoaster season, Miami was dominated by seventh-seeded Columbus in Game 1 at Nu Stadium. But coach Cristian "Kily" González insisted that an immediate exit would not be a failure.

"It would be a disappointment, but not a failure, this is football, after all," González, who took charge of Miami in September, told a news conference on Wednesday. "A true failure would be not trying at all. We are trying, sometimes well, sometimes not so well.

"That's just life: sometimes things go well, sometimes they don't."

Miami entered the playoffs as reigning MLS champion after defeating the Vancouver Whitecaps in last year's final. But the team is no stranger to first-round elimination, having fallen to Atlanta United in three games in 2024 despite setting a then-points record during the regular season.

"I know that, as a team, and as the reigning champions, it is our responsibility and our obligation to advance," González added. "It's not about feeling pressured. It's about recognizing where we stand and knowing we are prepared to go all the way.

"I don't look at it in terms of failure; I always envision us moving forward. I said as much after our last match, and I remain convinced that's how it will play out. We've prepared as best we could, even with the rain preventing us from training on the pitch, we've already put in the necessary work."

While a star-studded lineup led by back-to-back MLS Golden Boot winner Lionel Messi increases expectations in Miami, González said it also adds to the motivation for its rivals.

"Everyone wants to beat us," he said. "Every team plays differently against us; why? Because you have the world's number one, and because you know the repercussions that brings, so we have to come to terms with that."

"You have to accept that every team will try to beat you by any means necessary, no matter what. If you look at matches against other opponents, the game is played differently; against us, it's a whole other story, and you have to grasp that.

"So you have to be prepared, knowing that we're facing a final, our last chance, we're well aware of that."

stories.headline: WNBA players elect Elizabeth Williams as union president
stories.summary: Sky center Elizabeth Williams was elected president of the Women's National Basketball Players Association and will replace Nneka Ogwumike, who had been in the role since 2016.
stories.body:
Chicago Sky center Elizabeth Williams was elected president of the Women's National Basketball Players Association and will replace Nneka Ogwumike, who retired after being in the role since 2016.

Williams, who will serve out the final two years of Ogwumike's term that began earlier this year, was picked by players on Tuesday over Breanna Stewart of the New York Liberty and Gabby Williams of the Golden State Valkyries, a source with knowledge of the ballot told ESPN.

A 12-year veteran, Williams joined the WNBPA executive committee in 2018 and served four two-year terms. She has been at the bargaining table for two CBAs, including the most recent agreement that raised maximum player salaries to over $1 million.

"One of my main goals as president is to increase the engagement of the younger members of this union," Williams said in a statement to WNBPA player representatives. "I know the value of diverse voices in these conversations. We may not always agree, but I want to make sure every player knows that her voice is being heard.

"This is the strength of our union. I am grateful for what we have accomplished over these last few years, and I'm excited about the potential for a new opportunity to serve."

The WNBA will also have a new face leading the league office as commissioner Cathy Engelbert is retiring at the end of the year. A search for her replacement is ongoing.

Williams will lead the executive committee comprised of Napheesa Collier (1st vice president), Veronica Burton (secretary), Chelsea Gray (treasurer), and three additional vice presidents: Alysha Clark, Ezi Magbegor, and Maya Caldwell.

Burton, Gray, Magbegor and Caldwell join the executive committee for the first time.

"These election results reflect the strength of our union and the power of player leadership," WNBPA executive director Terri Carmichael Jackson said in a statement. "Congratulations to Elizabeth and each of our newly elected and returning Executive Committee members, whose collective experience, diverse perspectives, and commitment will help guide the WNBPA into its next chapter.

"As we turn our focus to implementing our transformational CBA and building on the progress our members have fought so hard to achieve, our greatest strength remains our unity, our democratic process, and our unwavering commitment to one another."

Williams, who was selected fourth overall in the 2015 WNBA draft out of Duke and was the 2016 Most Improved Player, becomes president after a lengthy period of stability in union leadership.

Ogwumike, the outgoing WNBPA president, announced her WNBA retirement during the 2026 season. An 11-time All-Star and the 2016 MVP, Ogwumike has served as WNBPA president since 2016, presiding over two collective bargaining agreement negotiations and shaping the social justice activism that defined the player body during her tenure.

stories.headline: Heeney headlines returning Swans at pre-season training
stories.summary: After months of off-field turmoil in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal, the Sydney Swans have welcomed back four AFL players for pre-season training.
stories.body:
The Sydney Swans have welcomed back their embattled AFL quartet to training after months of off-field turmoil following the Pullman Hotel scandal.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice signalled their intent to resurrect their playing careers by taking part in the club's first-to-fourth-year pre-season training on Monday.

High-profile forward Tom Papley was also in attendance at Sydney's Bat and Ball Oval after being slapped with a three-game ban by the AFL for a positive roadside drug test.

Monday's session marked the first time Heeney, Warner, Bice and Jordon have officially trained with the Swans since serving a season-ending suspension for what the club termed a "serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

That AFL-endorsed suspension was also served by now-North Melbourne player Nick Blakey.

Separate from the bans, Heeney, Warner, Jordon and Blakey were under investigation after three women made reports of sexual assault to Victoria Police.

Police have since confirmed the players would not be charged due to insufficient evidence.

Civil claims are still being prepared against relevant parties.

Monday's session was a relaxed affair, with the club also welcoming draftees Caylen Murray, Mason McGroder, Mitchell Knevitt and Brady Wright.

Players undertook the usual pre-season conditioning programs, doing running drills before moving on to contest work and a short match simulation.

It wasn't the first time Heeney, Warner, Jordon and Rice had trained with teammates, having done informal sessions at Centennial Park.

Papley, one of the team's most experienced players, returned to training as he prepares to face Waverley Local Court for driving with a suspended licence on November 26.

The 30-year-old was pulled over by NSW Police for a random roadside drug test on November 2, with checks revealing his licence was suspended due to non-payment of a parking fine.

The initial roadside test returned a positive reading, and a secondary sample of oral fluid was taken.

That secondary sample returned a positive roadside test for the presence of cocaine and MDMA.

On top of his AFL ban for conduct unbecoming, Papley was fined $722 by police and his licence will be suspended for three months.

Papley spent most of Monday's training session with the rehabilitation group alongside fellow forwards Logan McDonald and Hayden McLean after undergoing surgery on both knees.

He suffered a grade-two medial collateral ligament strain in his right knee in the club's preliminary final loss to Fremantle, before undergoing an arthroscopy on his left knee to address a historic issue.

Papley will miss all pre-season matches and the club's opening rounds against Geelong, Essendon and GWS.

stories.headline: 'Little disappointing': Munster makes call on Storm offer
stories.summary: Melbourne's fight to keep Cameron Munster and Harry Grant has been made harder after the former rejected the club's latest offer.
stories.body:
Cameron Munster has declared all options are on the table after officially rejecting a deal to stay in Melbourne and labelling the Storm's latest offer as "disappointing".

With Melbourne already facing a battle to retain Harry Grant, the Storm are now officially fighting a retention war on two fronts after Munster's call.

The Melbourne superstar admitted on Tuesday that Grant's future could play a role in his own call, as well as Craig Bellamy's impending retirement at the end of 2027.

As it stands Munster will not take up an offer from the Storm that is understood to have been for one year with an option for a second.

"I have declined it," the Queensland State of Origin captain said at a Maroons sponsor announcement with Westpac.

"I am not saying I am going to leave Melbourne. Just with the terms and conditions that they put out to me, it is probably something that is a little disappointing.

"But it's a business, I am not stupid."

Munster admitted his own form had not been good enough for the Storm last season as they missed the finals for the first time in his career.

And in turn, the 32-year-old conceded the offer may have been as a result of that.

"That (offer) just makes my job a little bit harder. But it's also a bit of a challenge saying I am not where I need to be," he said.

"Maybe I need to be a little bit better to earn that contract that we're looking from.

"And maybe it is a little bit of a kick up the bum from them. I am not too sure where we'll go from here but all options are open at the moment."

Munster's rejection comes after Grant met with Gold Coast officials last Friday and officially received an offer to join the Titans.

It is understood Melbourne's offer for the Queensland dummy-half will either be worth similar or more than the Titans.

But Gold Coast are hopeful of luring the hooker north, given his relationship with ex-Maroons assistant coach Josh Hannay and prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui.

The Titans officially released AJ Brimson to the PNG Chiefs on Tuesday on a three-year deal, with the money from the centre used to help pursue Grant.

NSW prop Stefano Utoikamanu is also off contract at Melbourne at the end of next year and has also been linked to the Sydney Roosters.

At the same time Bellamy's retirement at the end of next season is proving a challenge for the Storm, given he is like a father figure to Munster.

"When you look at someone like Craig as a coach, he is a great coach and I have so much respect and have admired him for such a long time," Munster said.

"It's going to be different at the club. I'm not too sure where the club wants to go with all that stuff.

"I don't know who they are going to get and I'm sure it will be a daunting job coming after him."

Munster also confirmed he will likely follow the Cameron Smith route and give away representative football at some point to focus on club duties.

"It definitely has (crossed my mind)," Munster said.

"The hard thing for me is giving up the captaincy.

"Once I start declining (I will look at it) and I thought I was declining. But after my last few games for the World Cup I am pretty confident I can get back to that."
